newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-European chemical industry seen stronger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European chemical industry seen stronger.

text.p: Western Europe's chemical industry faces better times in 1997 with rising production and demand but it lags behind the rival U.S. sector in competitive strength, according to industry reports published on Wednesday.
"The near term outlook for the chemical industry in Europe has improved significantly compared with last year," the European Chemical Industry Council (CEFIC) said in a statement.
However, the industry body added that the better business climate did not "remove the necessity to address the important structural issues which still face the industry."
Production of chemicals, including pharmaceuticals, is expected to grow by more than three percent in 1997 following an increase of less than two percent this year.

"There is already evidence of an upward trend, with output in the second half 1996 growing at an annual rate of over five percent, a sharp rebound from the weak performance registered in the first six months," CEFIC said.
Based on production and trade forecasts, demand for chemicals would also rise by more than three percent in 1997, considerably faster than this year.
The better figures are due to more economic growth as well as buoyant exports and changes in chemical stocks.
In line with this, Western Europe producer prices are expected to recover after an estimated 1.7 percent fall in 1996.

"To a large degree the fall in prices has come to an end and prices have either flattened out or are beginning to rise," it said, forecasting a 1997 rise of one percent, "with a strong probability that the increase will be higher than projected."
The outlook for investments and employment is less rosy.

Investments are expected to rise a solid 6.7 percent in 1996. However, this is still below last year's growth rate and for 1997 initial indications suggest that that the rise in capital spending will be between two and three percent.
The general trend for employment continues to be downward with the industry losing more than 300,000 jobs to roughly 1,7 million jobs since 1990.
"This year the figure is down by nearly two percent and the forecasts point to a similar reduction in 1997," CEFIC said.
A separate publication offered a gloomy assessment of the competitiveness of the European industry compared with the one in the United States.
The European industry is less profitable, struggles with higher energy and labour costs and with lower productivity, the Barometer of competitiveness said, using data for 1995.
"It appears that the chemical industry is significantly less profitable on the European side of the Atlantic whatever measure of profitability used," it said.
Espcially, net return on equity -- a key indicator for shareholders -- was about twice higher for U.S. chemical firms. "And 1995 was by no means exceptional in this respect," it said.
Energy costs are one third higher in Europe than in the United States and unit labour costs almost 40 percent higher.
To address the industry's competitiveness problems, the CEFIC report called for a reduction of labour costs and said the industry should aim at raising labour productivity.
"This presupposes higher rates of investment over a lengthy period of time in order to catch up with U.S. levels of capital intensity," it said.
Offering hope of a better development, CEFIC said economic and monetary union should boost industry competitiveness.
